catalog_quote: When following Hyman (2006), as well as in the traditional categorization of word prosodic systems, Beaver would be considered a tone language (for more discussion of the tonology of Beaver cf section 3.3.2 on page 57). ... Beaver, like many Athabaskan languages, has developed lexical tone as a reflex of syllables that were historically produced with a constricted glottis. These syllables now bear a lexical high tone in NAB, while the others are lexically low. Thus the dialect that is the object of this study is a “high-marking” language in Athabaskanist terminology. ... NAB has a high (H), a low (L) and a falling tone (HL) in its inventory. The falling tone being either historically or morphologically complex. ... An important morphological distinction that prevails in Athabaskan phonology is that between prefixes and stems. sweep_summary: Beaver (beav1236) is in the catalog as 'tonal' on the strength of Schwiertz 2009 p. 18. the list of works with stress in the title held a single item, Schwiertz 2009 itself (Glottolog 307383, already listed). I downloaded the open PDF from the Cologne repository, ledgered) and verified the catalog quotation verbatim on p. 18. The work confirms the classification: NAB is 'a full tone language where the TBU is the syllable' (p. 64), with lexical H/L/HL (sec. 3.3.2, pp. 57-60); stress 'does not play a role here' (p. 89) and no stress rule is ever proposed, only phonetic stem-vs-prefix strengthening (pp. 114, 121). Two further Beaver sources already held by the project from an earlier reading were read: Miller 2013 (UW PhD, phonetics of tone in Doig and Halfway dialects) confirms 'tonal' and is explicitly agnostic on stress (p. 129: needs 'a much more refined study'; p. 320 speculates stems may attract stress in Halfway; fn. 28 cites Leer 2005 for prefix-initial stress in one word, [ˈdə.ne] 'person'); the Randoja 1990 scanned excerpt (HRB Phonology ch. 4, ~10 pp.) is silent on stress. Nothing contradicts the catalog; the p. 64 passage is a useful supplementary locator but does not supersede the current deciding source (same work). No paywalled or print-only items remain; nothing to acquire at high priority. the full Randoja 1990 dissertation (uOttawa) would be the one remaining place to check for an explicit Halfway River Beaver stress statement (low priority).

new_statements.quote: In concluding this chapter, we will briefly adress the question what type of tone languages Beaver belongs to. When considering the possible combinations of tones for monosyllabic words in table 3.5, one can observe that the occurrence of the falling tone is somewhat restricted. Nevertheless, NAB should be classed with Donohue (1997) as a syllable tone language or with Hyman (2006) as a full tone language where the TBU is the syllable. In longer word forms in the verbal paradigm, one can see how tones are linked to affixes or stems and move around in the word with them. [p. 64] ... Other factors besides prosodic position (and stress which does not play a role here) can also have strengthening effects. [p. 89]
new_statements.citation: Schwiertz, Gabriele. 2009. Intonation & Prosodic Structure in Beaver (Athabaskan) - Explorations on the language of the Danezaa. PhD dissertation, Universität zu Köln.
new_statements.locator: p. 64 (conclusion of ch. 3 'Beaver'), supplemented by p. 88-89 (sec. 5.1)
new_statements.reading: Northern Alberta Beaver is a full (syllable-TBU) tone language with lexical H, L and a restricted falling HL tone; tones are lexically attached to affixes and stems and travel with them. Word stress is not posited for Beaver anywhere in the work and is explicitly said not to play a role; the only prominence described is phonetic stem-initial strengthening (pp. 114, 121), not culminative word stress. This confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and adds the precise classification (full tone language, TBU = syllable, three-way H/L/HL contrast).

sources.note: The dissertation is an intonation study of Northern Alberta Beaver (NAB, Doig/Blueberry; 'high-marking' dialect). It never posits word stress for Beaver: the only word-prosodic classification given is 'tone language' (Hyman 2006 sense; p. 18) refined on p. 64 to a 'full tone language where the TBU is the syllable' with H, L and (restricted) falling HL tones (sec. 3.3.2, pp. 57-60; tonal minimal pair sadyéé' 'my horn' vs sadyee' 'my food', yaa 'sky' vs yáá' 'louse'). sources.note: The only other prosody monograph on Beaver in Glottolog; instrumental tone study of Doig (H-marked) and Halfway (L-marked) dialects; confirms 'tonal' and explicitly flags word stress in Dane-zaa as unstudied (possible stem stress in Halfway raised only as speculation) — worth adding as a second ref/caution on the record.

sources.quote: p. 196: "(2) Disjunct prefix and Stem properties ... (c) Vowels have fixed lexical tone ... (3) Conjunct prefix properties ... (c) Most vowels have no fixed tone in surface forms"
sources.note: The excerpt held by the project (only ~10 pages of the phonology chapter) contains no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent' or 'prominence'; it describes lexical tone as fixed on disjunct prefixes and stems and absent on conjunct prefixes in Halfway River Beaver (the L-marking dialect). Silent on word stress in the pages read; the rest of the dissertation was not read here.
